query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) into a titanium‐nickel high‐entropy alloy (HEA) – where Ti and Ni are primary constituents – will improve the alloy’s mechanical performance at elevated temperatures by enhancing solid solution strengthening and stabilizing its microstructure against impurity‐induced segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, equiatomic or near‐equiatomic Ti–Ni high‐entropy alloy produced by conventional casting or melting methods (without Mo), in a solid-solution state that shows softening under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 5–10 at% Mo (by partial substitution of either Ti or Ni) to maintain single-phase stability while increasing the overall melting point and solid solution hardening effect.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1200 °C) in an inert (e.g., argon) or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation; mechanical tests such as high-temperature tensile or creep tests over extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo atoms, being refractory and having a sizeable atomic radius difference relative to Ti and Ni, increase lattice distortion and hinder dislocation motion while also reducing impurity-driven phase segregation at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Mo addition boosts the intrinsic high-temperature yield strength through enhanced solid solution strengthening and may suppress the diffusion of deleterious impurity interstitials (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen) that otherwise lead to phase segregation and softening. This stabilizes the single-phase structure under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline Ti–Ni HEA (without Mo), the Mo-containing alloy is expected to exhibit a higher yield strength, reduced creep rate, and improved resistance to thermal softening during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: A titanium-nickel high-entropy alloy without Mo addition, which under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing shows more pronounced softening and reduced mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect of Mo is anticipated only when its concentration is kept within a range (approximately 5–10 at%) that preserves the single-phase solid-solution structure. The predicted improvement applies primarily under high-temperature conditions (800–1200 °C) and long-term testing in controlled atmospheres; outside these boundaries, the effect or phase stability may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Mo concentration and its possible interactions with the principal constituents (Ti and Ni) remain to be precisely determined. There is also uncertainty whether Mo addition might provoke any unexpected secondary phase formation if processing conditions are not carefully controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples using identical processing conditions: one set of the baseline Ti–Ni HEA and one set modified with 5–10 at% Mo. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., creep and tensile tests at 1000 °C in an argon atmosphere) over extended periods. Conduct pre- and post-test microstructural analyses (using electron microscopy and phase identification tools) to assess phase stability and segregation.
measurements: Phase composition and grain boundary chemistry before/after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 10% increase in yield strength or reduction in creep rate) compared to the baseline Ti–Ni HEA, or if additional Mo induces detrimental secondary phase formation or instability under the testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
